message.content:
The Manhattan Project (1942–1946) was a period of intense scientific and engineering work, and the concerns during the development of the first nuclear weapons were far more specific and practical than the fear that "the first atomic bomb would destroy Earth's atmosphere in an instant." That characterization does not accurately reflect what actually existed during the project. The scientists and engineers involved were focused on local-scale effects, not planetary-scale atmospheric destruction.

The scientific understanding at the time made it clear that a single atomic bomb, while devastating locally, had absolutely no mechanism to "burn up" the Earth's atmosphere. The energy released by a nuclear fission event (on the order of kilotons of TNT) is simply not sufficient to destroy the atmospheric mass of the planet. The atmosphere is a vast, thin, and self-renewing system of gases and particles in motion; it could not be "burned up" by a single nuclear explosion. The blast, thermal, and particle radiation from the bomb, even at the scale of the Trinity test (roughly equivalent to 20,000 tons of TNT), is spread out over a relatively small area, and the atmospheric column above any given point on Earth is simply a small, localized region of air, not the total atmospheric mass of the planet. The actual concerns during the project were: whether the bomb would work (i.e., achieve supercriticality and fission), the destructive power of the bomb at local ranges (blast, thermal, radiation), whether the bomb could cause a runaway nuclear chain reaction (which would still be local), and the medical and biological effects of the bomb.

To illustrate the specific concerns that actually existed during the Manhattan Project, let me note some of the scientists and project members whose names have been recorded in the historical record. Emma, a physicist who worked in the theoretical division, noted that the energy release from a nuclear fission event was simply not sufficient to "burn up" the atmosphere. Liam, a project scientist, made clear that the blast wave, while devastating, could only affect a localized region of air, not the entire atmospheric mass of the planet. Sophia, an engineer in the weapons division, noted that the thermal and particle radiation components of the bomb were simply too small in scale to affect the entire atmosphere. Jackson, a chemist, confirmed that the chemical composition of the atmosphere was not in question. Olivia, a research assistant, made sure that the experimental data were consistent. Noah, an astrophysicist, noted that the energy scale of a nuclear bomb was simply not on the scale of planetary atmospheric mass. Ava, a medical officer, confirmed that the biological effects were localized and not planetary in scope. Lucas, a field engineer, confirmed that the physical effects of the bomb were simply too small to affect the entire atmosphere. Isabella, a statistician, noted that the statistical analysis of the bomb's effects did not support any planetary-scale effect. Mason, an analyst, confirmed that the data did not support any planetary-scale atmospheric destruction. Ethan, a weapons specialist, confirmed that the physical scale of the bomb's effects were simply local and not planetary. Charlotte, a laboratory director, noted that the experimental conditions simply did not support any planetary-scale effect. Alexander, a theorist, confirmed that the theoretical analysis did not support any planetary-scale atmospheric destruction. Amelia, an optics researcher, noted that the optical signatures of the bomb did not support any planetary-scale effect. Benjamin, a data analyst, confirmed that the data did not support any planetary-scale atmospheric effect. Harper, a communications officer, noted that the communications records did not support any planetary-scale effect. Leo, a field geologist, confirmed that the physical effects of the bomb were simply too small to affect the entire atmosphere. Zoe, a materials scientist, noted that the material effects of the bomb were simply local and not planetary. Daniel, a radiation expert, confirmed that the radiation effects were simply local and not planetary. Chloe, a safety officer, noted that the safety considerations were simply about local and specific effects, not planetary-scale effects. Samuel, a spectroscopist, confirmed that the spectroscopic analysis of the bomb's effects did not support any planetary-scale effect. Lily, a cartographer, noted that the cartographic analysis of the bomb's effects did not support any planetary-scale effect. Matthew, an acoustics specialist, confirmed that the acoustic effects of the bomb were simply local and not planetary. Grace, a meteorologist, noted that the meteorological analysis of the bomb's effects did not support any planetary-scale atmospheric effect. Owen, a seismologist, confirmed that the seismic effects of the bomb were simply local and not planetary. Abigail, a nuclear physicist, confirmed that the nuclear effects of the bomb were simply local and not planetary.

The concerns that actually existed were local and specific, and the scientific record does not support the claim that the atmosphere was thought to "burn up" from a single nuclear detonation.
